newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS - German tax reforms include VAT rise-sources.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - German tax reforms include VAT rise-sources.

text.p: A German tax reform commission plans to propose a two percentage point increase in value-added tax to help finance a comprehensive income tax reform, commission sources said on Monday.

The outlines of the reform plan took harder shape at a closed commission meeting over the weekend in Wildbad Kreuth, the sources said. The panel, headed by Finance Minister Theo Waigel, is due to make its proposals to Chancellor Helmut Kohl's cabinet on December 11.

Waigel, under pressure from junior coalition partners the Free Democrats (FDP) to accelerate the process, said parts of the reform may be implemented in 1998, but the bulk of it will have to wait until the next year.
Kohl's Christian Democrats also agreed to an FDP demand to cut the unpopular solidarity tax two percentage points to 5.5 percent in 1998.

Juergen Moellemann, head of the FDP in North Rhine-Westphalia, told the Bild newspaper: "After talks with coalition leaders I am sure that the solidarity tax will be cut two percentage points on January 1, 1998."
FDP chief Wolfgang Gerhardt said the comprehensive tax reform must bring a net tax cut for the public.

Planned reductions in tax rates could depress government revenues by about 90 billion marks ($58.4 billion), but Bonn aims to claw back about 30 billion marks of that by raising VAT and a further 30 billion by eliminating as many deductions, exemptions and loopholes as possible, the commission sources said.
The top income tax rate will be cut to 35 or 40 percent from the current 53 percent, and the lowest rate to about 20 percent.

The commission is also considering reducing the corporate tax on retained earnings to 40 percent from 45 percent, and cutting the top rate on commercial income to 42 percent from 47 percent, but it would limit write-offs for depreciation and reserves, the Handelsblatt newspaper reported.
Differences of opinion remain on how best to tax profits from the sale of assets such as stocks and real estate, the sources said.
The income tax reform plan would reduce the basic deduction for employed persons to 1,000 marks or 1,200 marks from the current 2,000 marks a year.
It would broaden the commuting deduction to apply to all, not just those who drive their own cars, but at a much lower rate of about 0.20 marks per kilometer, down from 0.70 marks.

Unemployment benefits and other non-salary compensation would be fully subject to tax, though personal income-tax deductions would mean such income remained largely tax-free except in cases of taxpayers with other supplemental income.
Tax exemptions for Sunday, holiday and night pay would be eliminated, as would most exemptions for legal settlements and other extraordinary income.

The solidarity tax, aimed at helping to finance the reconstruction of formerly communist east Germany, was to have been cut one point in January 1997 and a further point in 1998, but that plan was recently scrapped to fill a 1997 budget gap. ($1=1.5414 Mark)
